In plain words

Attackers are trying to abuse a serious flaw in WSO2 software used to manage and route application connections, allowing them to create fake login passes that appear to grant administrator access. Organizations using affected WSO2 API Manager, API Control Plane, Traffic Manager, or Universal Gateway versions could have their accounts and connected application systems exposed. This could let attackers access secret keys and passwords, read sensitive information moving through the systems, and reach internal services, so affected users should install the available fixes quickly.

Summary
WSO2 API Manager and related products are under active exploitation for CVE-2026-5430, a critical JWT signature-validation bypass that lets attackers forge administrator tokens and potentially take over accounts. Organizations should immediately apply WSO2’s available fixes and updates.

A critical flaw in WSO2 API Manager, CVE-2026-5430, is being actively targeted, according to watchTowr. The issue involves improper verification of a cryptographic signature in JSON Web Tokens, which can allow authentication to be bypassed. WSO2 said tokens signed with unsupported algorithms may be accepted, potentially allowing unauthorized access, administrative-account compromise, and full account takeover.

watchTowr’s honeypot network captured forged JWTs with built-in administrator privileges on September 13, 2026. The affected software includes specified versions of WSO2 API Manager, API Control Plane, Traffic Manager, and Universal Gateway. Successful use of the flaw could provide access to API backend endpoints, credentials, consumer keys, and application secrets, while also allowing interception of sensitive data and interaction with internal services. WSO2 has released fixes through community pull requests and designated update levels for support subscription holders, and users are advised to apply them as soon as possible.

  • The authentication failure is especially severe because the service accepts tokens signed with algorithms it does not support, rather than rejecting them.
  • The observed forged tokens already contained administrator privileges, indicating attempts to obtain high-level access rather than merely bypass a standard user login.
  • Because the affected software sits in the path of API requests to internal systems, a successful compromise could enable interception of sensitive data while it moves between services.
  • WSO2 has made fixes available both through public community pull requests and through specific update levels for support subscription holders, giving affected organizations clear remediation paths.
Key Points
  • 01CVE-2026-5430 is a critical WSO2 JWT authentication flaw that allows unauthorized access when tokens are signed with unsupported algorithms but are accepted anyway.
  • 02watchTowr reported active exploitation attempts, including forged JWT tokens with administrator privileges captured by its honeypot network on September 13, 2026.
  • 03The affected products include WSO2 API Manager versions 4.1.0 through 4.6.0, along with specified versions of WSO2 API Control Plane, Traffic Manager, and Universal Gateway.
  • 04WSO2 has released fixes through community pull requests and update levels for WSO2 Support Subscription Holders.
  • 05According to watchTowr, successful exploitation could expose API backend endpoints, credentials, consumer keys, application secrets, sensitive data in transit, and internal services.

In plain words

Attackers are actively abusing a serious flaw in ConnectWise ScreenConnect, a remote-access tool used by IT teams to troubleshoot and maintain computers. The flaw can let someone with limited access move or run files on another computer during a remote session without permission or confirmation. U.S. government agencies were told to fix affected systems within three days, and more than 1,000 internet-exposed systems were still unpatched, creating risks for the many IT providers and managed service companies that rely on the product.

Summary
CISA says attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-84869, a critical ConnectWise ScreenConnect authorization flaw that can enable unauthorized file transfer and execution during remote sessions. Organizations should upgrade to ScreenConnect 26.6.5 or later immediately, as more than 1,000 exposed instances remain unpatched.

Attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-84869, a critical ConnectWise ScreenConnect flaw involving improper privilege management and missing authorization. CISA added the issue to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog and ordered U.S. federal agencies to secure affected systems within three days. The flaw affects ScreenConnect clients and can enable file transfer or execution through active remote sessions without authorization or host confirmation.

ConnectWise issued temporary mitigation guidance on September 7, advising organizations to disable TransferFiles permissions, and later patched the flaw in ScreenConnect 26.6.5 and later. Shadowserver tracked more than 1,000 unpatched ScreenConnect instances exposed online, including 758 in North America and 180 in Europe. ScreenConnect has been repeatedly targeted: CISA has identified four actively exploited ScreenConnect flaws since 2024, and two have also been used in ransomware attacks.

ConnectWise says its services are used by more than 100,000 IT providers worldwide, including managed service providers and IT teams that use ScreenConnect for troubleshooting, patching, and system maintenance. The article also notes that Kimsuky and several ransomware groups exploited a different ScreenConnect flaw, CVE-2024-1709, in 2024. In March, ConnectWise addressed CVE-2026-3564, a signature-verification issue that could allow attackers to hijack unpatched ScreenConnect servers.

  • The flaw is especially urgent because it is already being used in attacks and can be abused with only basic privileges, without requiring user interaction.
  • Disabling TransferFiles permissions was ConnectWise's temporary safeguard before the patch, making that setting a directly relevant control for organizations unable to upgrade immediately.
  • ScreenConnect is a recurring target: since 2024, CISA has listed four of its flaws as actively exploited, and two were also used in ransomware attacks.
  • The exposure has broad downstream implications because ScreenConnect is used by more than 100,000 IT providers worldwide, including managed service providers that maintain other organizations' systems.

  • 02The missing-authorization and privilege-management flaw can allow attackers with basic privileges to transfer or execute files through active remote sessions without host confirmation.
  • 03ConnectWise patched the vulnerability in ScreenConnect version 26.6.5 and later, after initially recommending that organizations disable TransferFiles permissions as a temporary mitigation.
  • 04CISA ordered U.S. federal agencies to secure affected systems within three days because of ongoing attacks.

In plain words

Attackers are taking advantage of a serious flaw in the WooCommerce Wholesale Lead Capture add-on used by more than 6,000 WordPress websites. The flaw lets anyone upload harmful files that can give them control of a website, and more than 100,000 attempted break-ins have already been blocked. The article also reports similar serious flaws in The Events Calendar add-on, which is used on over 600,000 sites and could let attackers take over sites, steal sensitive information, or install harmful software.

Summary
Attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-27540 in WooCommerce Wholesale Lead Capture versions through 2.0.3.1 to upload PHP web shells and take over vulnerable WordPress sites. Site owners should update immediately and check for unexpected PHP files, especially in uploads directories.

Threat actors are actively exploiting CVE-2026-27540, a critical flaw in the WooCommerce Wholesale Lead Capture WordPress plugin, which has more than 6,000 active installations. The issue affects all plugin versions through 2.0.3.1 and allows unauthenticated attackers to upload arbitrary files, including PHP backdoors, potentially leading to remote code execution. Wordfence said it had blocked more than 100,000 exploit attempts since June 2026.

Observed attacks send crafted requests to WordPress’s /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php endpoint using the wwlc_file_upload_handler action, a forged file_settings parameter, and a malicious shell.php file. The uploaded web shell reports host details and provides a browser-based form for placing more malicious files on a compromised site. Site owners are advised to look for unexpected or newly created PHP files, particularly in upload directories, and review suspicious requests using that action.

The article also describes two critical unauthenticated remote-code-execution flaw chains in The Events Calendar plugin, which is installed on more than 600,000 websites. The flaws, CVE-2026-78159 and CVE-2026-78006, require comments to be enabled on an event page and the plugin’s option to show comments on event pages to be active. Wordfence warned that the chains can be triggered through pending-comment previews and could enable site takeover, sensitive-data theft, and malware deployment; StellarWP fixed them in versions 6.17.3.1 and 6.17.4.1, respectively.

  • The WooCommerce Wholesale Lead Capture flaw can be abused without an account because its file-upload function does not properly validate file types.
  • A successful upload can provide attackers with a browser-based tool to place further malicious files on a compromised WordPress site.
  • Site owners can look for suspicious activity by reviewing requests to /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php that use the wwlc_file_upload_handler action and by checking for newly created PHP files in upload directories.
  • The two The Events Calendar attack paths can be triggered through pending-comment previews without moderator approval when comments are enabled on event pages and the relevant plugin option is active.
  • One The Events Calendar flaw chain can reset an administrator password, allowing an attacker to upload a malicious plugin and take complete control of the site.
Key Points

  • 02Wordfence said it has blocked more than 100,000 exploit attempts targeting the WooCommerce Wholesale Lead Capture flaw since June 2026.
  • 03Observed attacks submit crafted requests to the wwlc_file_upload_handler action with a forged file_settings parameter and a malicious PHP file named shell.php.
  • 04The uploaded PHP web shell reports host details and provides a browser-based form for placing additional malicious files on a compromised WordPress site.
  • 05Wordfence also disclosed two critical unauthenticated remote-code-execution flaw chains affecting The Events Calendar, which StellarWP addressed in versions 6.17.3.1 and 6.17.4.1.

In plain words

A serious flaw in Issabel, software used to run business phone systems, is being actively abused. Because every installation used the same built-in secret, outsiders could impersonate authorized users and make the phone-system software run commands on its underlying computer without logging in. Organizations using Issabel could have their phone-system servers taken over, so they should install the available fix.

Summary
A critical Issabel Framework flaw, CVE-2026-89026, is being actively exploited to forge JWTs and remotely execute arbitrary commands as the Asterisk user without authentication. Organizations should apply Issabel’s August 2026 patch immediately.

A critical vulnerability in the Issabel Framework, CVE-2026-89026, is under active exploitation. The flaw has a CVSS v3.1 score of 9.8 and can let an unauthenticated remote attacker execute arbitrary operating-system commands. Issabel Framework is a web-based framework for open-source unified communications PBX software.

The issue stems from a hard-coded HS256 JSON Web Token signing key in the pbxapi index.php file that was identical across installations. Attackers can forge valid bearer tokens and call the /pbxapi/manager/originate endpoint with Asterisk’s System application parameter, causing commands to run as the Asterisk user. Issabel released a patch on August 1, 2026, replacing the built-in key with one stored in /etc/issabel.conf, and Shadowserver Foundation first observed exploitation on September 9, 2026.

  • Because the same built-in signing secret was used across every Issabel installation, a token forged for one vulnerable installation could be created without needing that installation’s own unique secret.
  • The available fix changes the signing secret from a hard-coded value to one stored locally in /etc/issabel.conf, making it specific to the installation rather than shared globally.
  • The patch was released on August 1, 2026, while Shadowserver Foundation first observed exploitation on September 9, 2026.
  • Although exploitation has been observed, the article states that the attackers, their methods, and the scale of the activity remain unknown.
Key Points
  • 01CVE-2026-89026 is a critical Issabel Framework vulnerability that allows unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary operating system commands.
  • 02The flaw stems from a hard-coded JWT signing key in the pbxapi index.php file that was identical across Issabel installations.
  • 03Attackers can forge bearer tokens and invoke the /pbxapi/manager/originate endpoint with Asterisk’s System application parameter to run commands as the Asterisk user.
  • 04Issabel released a patch on August 1, 2026, replacing the hard-coded JWT key with a key stored in /etc/issabel.conf.
  • 05Shadowserver Foundation first observed exploitation of the vulnerability on September 9, 2026, and users are advised to apply the latest fixes.

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-70756) Oracle WebLogic Server Takeover via T3 and IIOP

In plain words

Oracle has disclosed a serious flaw in WebLogic Server, software many organizations use to run business applications, that could let an outsider take complete control of a server without needing a login. The risk affects several supported WebLogic versions, especially systems that can be reached from the internet, including development and testing systems that may not be updated as promptly as production systems. This matters because compromised servers can expose or disrupt important services such as order management, logistics, identity services, and partner connections, so organizations should install Oracle’s available fixes and limit outside access until they do.

Summary
Oracle WebLogic Server CVE-2026-70756 is a critical pre-authentication flaw (CVSS 9.8) that can allow attackers with network access to T3 or IIOP ports to fully compromise affected servers. Organizations should urgently apply Oracle’s September 2026 CPU patches and restrict external access to T3 and IIOP, especially on TCP ports 7001 and 7002.

Oracle disclosed CVE-2026-70756, a critical vulnerability in the Core component of Oracle WebLogic Server, in its September 15, 2026 Critical Security Patch Update. The flaw has a CVSS v3.1 score of 9.8 and can let an unauthenticated attacker with network access use T3 or IIOP to compromise a server and take full control. Oracle lists high impacts to confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

Affected versions are 12.2.1.4.0, 14.1.1.0.0, 14.1.2.0.0, and 15.1.1.0.0, with patches available for all four versions. T3 and IIOP may be reachable on the same default listen ports used for HTTP traffic, including TCP ports 7001 and 7002, so an externally visible web application server can still accept these protocol requests. Until patching is confirmed, the article recommends identifying internet-facing WebLogic instances, restricting T3 and IIOP to trusted sources, disabling unneeded IIOP, monitoring for unexpected T3 handshakes, and reviewing load balancer forwarding rules.

  • WebLogic systems may expose the risky T3 and IIOP interfaces through the same ports used for normal web traffic, meaning a server that appears to be only a web application can still accept these connections on TCP ports 7001 and 7002.
  • Many exposed systems were identified by their service fingerprint rather than a confirmed software version, indicating that organizations may have more potentially affected WebLogic instances than their internal records show.
  • Development, testing, and staging WebLogic environments are particularly likely to be externally reachable while receiving less consistent patching than production systems.
  • Oracle provides the fix as a cumulative patch bundle for each installed WebLogic version rather than as an upgrade to a newer release, and patch availability for older versions can depend on the organization’s support contract.
  • Reviewing load balancer rules is an actionable priority because rules that forward an entire WebLogic listen port can unintentionally expose T3 and IIOP instead of limiting access to web traffic.
Key Points
  • 01CVE-2026-70756 is a critical Oracle WebLogic Server flaw with a CVSS v3.1 score of 9.8 that can allow an unauthenticated network attacker using T3 or IIOP to take full control of a server.
  • 02Oracle identifies WebLogic Server versions 12.2.1.4.0, 14.1.1.0.0, 14.1.2.0.0, and 15.1.1.0.0 as affected by CVE-2026-70756.
  • 03T3 and IIOP can be reachable on WebLogic’s default HTTP listen ports, including TCP ports 7001 and 7002, even when an instance appears externally to be an ordinary web application server.
  • 04Oracle released fixes for all four affected versions in its September 15, 2026 Critical Security Patch Update.
  • 05Until patching is confirmed, the article recommends inventorying internet-facing WebLogic systems, restricting T3 and IIOP access, disabling unneeded IIOP, and reviewing load balancer rules that forward full listen ports.

In plain words

A criminal operation linked to Brazil has been tricking people into opening files that look like bank receipts or invoices, then secretly adding harmful add-ons to their Chrome or Edge browser. These add-ons can steal passwords, login information, typed text, screenshots, and other browsing data, and can change what people see or where their clicks go. KREMLIN banking malware is infecting primarily Brazilian users and covertly installing malicious Chrome and Edge extensions by modifying Chromium profile settings and recreating their integrity checks. The AVSync-branded extensions steal credentials, cookies, session data, keystrokes, screenshots, and web traffic while giving attackers browser-level control.

Elastic Security Labs identified KREMLIN, a banking-malware toolkit linked to a Brazilian operation that has run at least seven campaigns since May 2025 impersonating 12 banks. The infection begins when a target opens a JavaScript file disguised as a bank receipt, invoice, payment record, or business document. After anti-sandbox checks, the malware displays a fake error while downloading Node.js, creating a scheduled task for persistence, and obtaining additional payload information from an Ethereum smart contract.

KREMLIN can install malicious Chrome and Edge extensions without user approval by copying them into browser profiles, enabling developer mode, and adding them to Chromium Secure Preferences. It retrieves the browser keys and regenerates the cryptographic checks needed to make the unauthorized extension appear valid. The AVSync-branded extension can steal browser data, passwords and other typed form text, screenshots, page source, cookies, session data, and HTTP request information, while also injecting content and redirecting clicks. Elastic confirmed 1,515 infected systems, almost all in Brazil, and disrupted the current campaign by registering a domain used by the malware as an anti-sandbox canary.

  • KREMLIN does not merely force-load a browser add-on; it obtains Chromium’s protection keys and recreates the checks that normally reveal unauthorized preference changes, allowing the extension to appear user-approved.
  • The operation used Ethereum smart contracts as locations for malware payload information and hid payloads inside JPEG images hosted through the Internet Archive service.
  • Elastic disrupted the active campaign by registering the domain used as an anti-sandbox check, causing the malware loader to stop on systems that would otherwise have met its infection conditions.
  • The malicious extension combines account-data theft with the ability to alter webpages and redirect clicks, giving operators both access to browser data and influence over a victim’s web activity.

The group also exploits Active Directory weaknesses and BlueKeep to move laterally, steal credentials, and potentially compromise domain controllers.

Kaspersky’s Global Emergency Response Team investigated several incidents involving NightEagle (APT-Q-95), a group active since at least 2023 that has expanded from targets in Asia to businesses in Russia. The attackers commonly entered corporate VPNs using compromised valid credentials, with connections traced to Russian IP addresses associated with Cloudflare WARP tunnels and European virtual infrastructure providers. They deployed the GhostContainer backdoor on Microsoft Exchange servers during initial access and later stages of the intrusion.

GhostContainer receives commands through Exchange request headers, can redirect network traffic, and attempts to evade Windows security monitoring by altering functions in AMSI and Windows event logging components. NightEagle used Microsoft dev tunnels, rdp2tcp, GitHub-hosted tools disguised as legitimate software, and Impacket’s atexec utility to maintain access and move through internal networks. In one incident, the group exploited the BlueKeep vulnerability, requested Kerberos tickets with unusual flags, and attempted Active Directory replication to obtain password hashes and ultimately compromise domain controllers and the victim’s Active Directory infrastructure.

  • NightEagle combined Microsoft dev tunnels with rdp2tcp to preserve remote access through legitimate services while avoiding additional suspicious open ports.

  • The group disguised tools in GitHub repositories and archives with legitimate-looking names, while the executable names inside the archives mimicked unrelated well-known software.
  • GhostContainer is designed to receive commands through Microsoft Exchange request headers and to weaken Windows security monitoring by altering functions in AMSI and Windows event logging components.
  • The attackers used long-lived Kerberos tickets, password-hash theft, and attempted Active Directory replication to establish persistence and potentially take control of an organization’s identity infrastructure.

Summary
Microsoft is investigating reports that Windows 11 KB5124008 can break Active Directory domain trust on some enterprise devices after reboot, preventing valid domain logins. Administrators suspect the Machine Identity Isolation/Credential Guard setting is involved, but Microsoft has not issued an official workaround.

Microsoft is investigating reports that the Windows 11 KB5124008 security update breaks domain trust relationships on some enterprise systems after installation and reboot. Affected computers can reject valid domain credentials, preventing users from signing in, while cached credentials may continue working offline. Administrators reported that uninstalling the update and repairing the computer’s secure channel restored access, but the issue returned when KB5124008 was reinstalled.

Reports indicate the failures may be related to the Windows Machine Identity Isolation feature, particularly when it is enabled in audit or enforcement mode. In enforcement mode, Windows moves the machine account secret into Credential Guard and removes the copy stored in LSA, which can affect the computer’s connection to Active Directory. Some administrators restored systems by setting the MachineIdentityIsolation registry value to 0, rebooting, and repairing the secure channel with PowerShell, but Microsoft has not confirmed the cause or issued an official workaround and warns that disabling the feature can also create domain-authentication problems.

  • The reported problem can appear as a password failure even when users’ credentials are valid, because the affected computer’s trust relationship with the domain has failed.
  • Offline cached sign-ins continuing to work indicates the reported failures are tied to communicating with the company domain rather than to users’ passwords.
  • Administrators reported that setting MachineIdentityIsolation to enforcement mode caused Windows to move the computer’s account secret into Credential Guard and remove its local copy from LSA.
  • Disabling Machine Identity Isolation is not a universally safe workaround: one administrator reported domain trust failures on systems that never installed KB5124008, and Microsoft warns that devices previously using enforcement mode may need to be removed from and rejoined to the domain.

In plain words

GitHub added a setting for its automated software-building service that lets project owners control whether a task can use or change stored build files. This helps prevent someone from slipping harmful files into shared storage so they run later in a more trusted task with access to sensitive information. The risk has already been linked to compromises involving Ultralytics, TanStack software packages, and the Cline project, affecting developers and people who use software built through GitHub. The change reduces one route for abuse, but it does not stop other dangers from running untrusted code in these automated tasks.

Summary
GitHub Actions introduced cache-mode to restrict cache reads and writes per workflow or job, reducing the risk that untrusted workflows poison caches later used by privileged builds. The feature adds read, write, write-only, and none modes, but does not mitigate other risks from running untrusted code or scripts in CI.

GitHub added cache-mode to GitHub Actions, allowing maintainers to limit cache access for individual workflows or jobs. The feature is intended to reduce cache poisoning, in which an attacker places malicious build files or dependencies into a shared cache for a trusted workflow to later restore and run. The article links this risk to the 2024 Ultralytics PyPI compromise and the May 2026 TanStack package compromise.

cache-mode provides four options: read, write, write-only, and none, with job-level settings taking precedence over workflow-level settings. Cache access is enforced by the cache service, and reusable workflows cannot receive more access than their caller grants. GitHub recommends none for AI agent workflows that process untrusted issue or pull-request text, but notes that the feature does not address other Actions risks such as checking out untrusted code, running package lifecycle scripts, or minting OIDC tokens.

  • Build provenance and Sigstore signatures can still validate a build that used a poisoned cache, because they confirm where and when the build ran rather than the integrity of cached inputs.
  • A reusable workflow cannot gain more cache access than its caller grants, preventing a called workflow from bypassing the caller's cache restrictions.
  • The write-only setting lets a trusted branch populate a cache without restoring any existing entry, a control added after public feedback.
  • GitHub warns when a low-trust event is explicitly granted write or write-only cache access because those settings can restore cache-poisoning risk.
  • Most untrusted triggers already received read-only cache defaults in June 2026; cache-mode adds finer per-job control, a complete cache block, and service-enforced restrictions.
Key Points
  • 01GitHub added cache-mode to GitHub Actions to control cache access at the workflow or job level and reduce cache-poisoning risk.
  • 02Cache poisoning can allow an attacker to place malicious build artifacts or dependencies in a shared Actions cache that a trusted workflow later restores and runs.
  • 03cache-mode supports read, write, write-only, and none settings, with job-level settings overriding workflow-level settings.
  • 04GitHub recommends cache-mode: none for AI agent workflows that process untrusted issue or pull-request text.
  • 05The feature does not address other GitHub Actions risks, including checking out untrusted code, running package lifecycle scripts, or minting OIDC tokens in a runner.

It is not an active incident or emergency patch, but it provides an actionable security control for widely used CI workflows.

The Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) received a report of an alleged personal-data breach carried out by an AI agent powered by a known large language model. The AEPD also noted that confirmation of AI use would not necessarily mean the underlying model, its provider’s infrastructure, or the model’s design had been compromised or intended to enable malicious activity.

In plain words

The article examines Atomic macOS (AMOS), a program that steals information from Mac computers after people are tricked by websites claiming to offer free or cracked software tools. Victims are told to copy and paste a command into the Mac Terminal app, which installs hidden files, asks for access to personal folders and apps, and can collect passwords, browser information, chat data, and cryptocurrency-wallet data. This matters because the program’s websites, file names, and internet servers change often, making it harder to block using a fixed list of known warning signs.

Summary
Atomic macOS (AMOS) stealer is an actively evolving macOS infostealer spread through malicious software-installation pages that trick users into pasting commands into Terminal. It establishes persistence, requests access to user data and applications, and exfiltrates credentials, browser data, messaging data, cryptocurrency-wallet information, and other files to changing command-and-control infrastructure.

Unit 42 analyzed an Atomic macOS (AMOS) stealer infection generated in a lab on Aug. 5, 2026, after a user followed instructions from a malicious website advertising a “macOS toolkit.” The site at getmacouscloud[.]com instructed the user to copy text into Terminal, which downloaded a Zsh script and launched a multi-stage installation process. The authors note that this copy-and-paste lure resembles ClickFix activity but does not meet their definition of a traditional ClickFix campaign because it did not use a fake CAPTCHA or clipboard-injection verification page.

The infection saved AMOS components in hidden-looking directories under the user’s Library/Application Support folder and requested the user’s password and permissions to control Finder and Notes and access Desktop and Documents files. It collected information into /tmp/out.zip, including data associated with browsers, messaging applications, cryptocurrency wallets, cloud tools, and shell history, then sent HTTP POST requests to a command-and-control server. The article emphasizes that AMOS infrastructure, file names, hashes, directory paths, and command-and-control addresses change frequently, while its overall collection and upload patterns remain consistent.

  • The article distinguishes this copy-and-paste lure from a traditional ClickFix campaign: it did not use a fake CAPTCHA or clipboard-injection verification page, even though it similarly directed the victim to run text in Terminal.
  • The initial downloaded Zsh script concealed its next stage as Base64-encoded, GZIP-compressed content, showing that the visible first-stage command was only part of a multi-stage installation chain.
  • The infected test Mac had no additional applications installed, yet the collected archive included paths for Binance, TonKeeper, AWS, Docker, FileZilla, and Google Cloud data, revealing the range of applications and data sources AMOS was designed to search for.
  • A comparison of infections only days apart found different command-and-control IP addresses while retaining similar data-upload URL patterns, indicating that behavioral patterns may remain useful even as domains, IPs, filenames, hashes, and storage paths change.
  • The malware used hidden-looking directory names resembling Apple-related locations under the user’s Application Support folder, which could make its persistent files less noticeable during a manual review.

In plain words

Researchers found a flaw in Parallels Desktop, software that lets Macs run Windows or Linux, which can allow a regular account on the same Mac to take complete control of it. It affects Macs with vulnerable Parallels Desktop 26 installations, including Intel Macs, while the stated fix is in version 27, which Intel Macs cannot install. This matters because harmful software or a compromised low-level account could use the flaw to gain the highest level of access and remain on the computer even after an update.

Summary
A local privilege-escalation flaw in Parallels Desktop 26 can let any non-admin Mac user gain root through argument injection in the appliance-install service. JFrog says Parallels Desktop 27 fixes it, but Intel Macs cannot install that version and currently lack a confirmed patched release.

JFrog disclosed ParaShells, tracked as CVE-2026-90894, a Parallels Desktop flaw that can allow a non-administrator local Mac account to execute code as root. The issue affects the Mac host rather than Windows or Linux virtual machines running within Parallels. It requires code to already be running locally under a normal user account and cannot be used remotely over a network.

JFrog found that Parallels’ root-level dispatcher service exposes a world-writable local socket and constructs an appliance-extraction command in a way that permits injected tar options through a crafted destination folder name. Its demonstration used tar’s --use-compress-program option to run a program as root, and no virtual machine needed to be active. JFrog identifies Parallels Desktop 27 as fixed, but version 27 supports only Apple silicon Macs; Intel Macs must stay on the 26.x line, which JFrog says does not include the relevant change, leaving no confirmed patch for those systems.

  • The flaw does not require a virtual machine to be running, because the vulnerable root-level Parallels service is already installed and available on a normal installation.
  • The stated patch timeline is unclear: JFrog says version 27.0.0 fixed the issue on 1 September 2026, while Parallels release notes list 27.0.0 on 25 August and 27.0.1 on 1 September.
  • Intel Mac users face a patch gap because Parallels directs them to remain on version 26, but JFrog says the extract-command change is absent from that product line, including 26.4.2.
  • A software update may not remove an attacker who already gained root access, since JFrog notes that root-level access can be used to establish persistence through launchd.

In plain words

Researchers showed that someone who has already gained powerful administrator access to a Microsoft Entra organization can add a fake sign-in check that looks like a real Microsoft password page. Employees may enter their password again during a normal-looking login, allowing the attacker to collect it while still letting the login succeed without an error. This affects organizations using Entra that allow these outside sign-in providers, because simply changing stolen passwords will not stop the trap unless the fake provider is removed first.

Summary
Varonis researchers demonstrated TrustSink, a post-compromise technique in which a privileged attacker registers a rogue Microsoft Entra External Authentication Method that mimics a Microsoft password prompt, captures plaintext passwords, and returns valid signed tokens to complete MFA sign-ins. Defenders should monitor Entra authentication-policy and application changes, remove suspicious providers before resetting passwords, and restrict privileged identity roles.

Varonis Threat Labs demonstrated TrustSink, a technique that turns a trusted Microsoft Entra External Authentication Method into a persistent password-collection trap. An attacker with a Global Administrator or Authentication Policy Administrator account can register a rogue provider that displays a convincing copy of a Microsoft password prompt during a legitimate sign-in. The provider captures the password entered by the user, then returns a valid signed token so the login completes normally without an error.

The technique is a post-compromise persistence method because it requires privileged access to modify Entra’s Authentication Methods Policy and register associated application artifacts. Changing a stolen password alone does not stop the threat, because the rogue provider remains in the sign-in flow and can collect the replacement password during the user’s next login. Defenders should investigate unauthorized external authentication-provider registrations, related application, service-principal, and consent changes, as well as unfamiliar provider issuers and hardware-key claims in sign-in logs; they should remove the provider before resetting affected credentials.

  • The credential trap persists through password resets because the malicious external provider remains embedded in the authentication flow and can collect the new password at the next sign-in.
  • The attack can appear especially convincing because the second password request occurs immediately after the user has entered their real password on Microsoft’s own sign-in site, making the repeated request seem routine.
  • Microsoft Entra validates the provider’s signed response against the registered public key, but the research found it does not verify what page the provider showed the user before issuing that response.
  • An unfamiliar external-provider issuer paired with hardware-key sign-in claims is a particularly strong detection signal, because the provider’s issuer URL and claims are recorded in sign-in logs.
  • The deployment creates a connected audit trail of an application registration, service principal, consent grant, and authentication-policy change, which defenders can use to investigate suspicious identity infrastructure changes.
Key Points
  • 01Varonis Threat Labs demonstrated TrustSink, a technique that uses a rogue Microsoft Entra External Authentication Method to present a fake password page during a legitimate sign-in flow and capture plaintext passwords.
  • 02An attacker needs a Global Administrator or Authentication Policy Administrator account to register the rogue provider, making TrustSink a post-compromise technique.
  • 03The rogue provider can return a valid signed token to Entra after collecting a password, allowing the victim's sign-in to complete normally without an error.
  • 04Resetting a captured password alone does not remove the rogue provider, which can capture the replacement password at the user’s next sign-in.
  • 05Defenders should watch for unauthorized Authentication Methods Policy changes, suspicious application and service-principal registrations, unfamiliar sign-in issuers reporting hardware-key claims, and scripted Microsoft Graph activity.

In plain words

Ukraine’s parliament approved tougher punishments for people who set up, run, work for, or recruit others into scam call centers, with prison terms of seven to 12 years possible. The move followed allegations that officials took bribes to protect these operations from law enforcement, leading to the removal of the country’s prosecutor general. These call centers trick people in Ukraine and other countries, including the United States, into sending money, making fake investments, or handing over access to their bank accounts. Summary
Ukraine’s parliament passed legislation imposing up to 12 years in prison for operating, staffing, or recruiting for scam call centers, following allegations that Prosecutor General’s Office officials accepted bribes to protect such operations. The measure awaits President Zelenskyy’s signature amid broader law-enforcement crackdowns on fraud centers targeting victims in Ukraine and abroad.

Ukraine’s parliament approved legislation imposing tougher criminal penalties for fraudulent call-center activity and the theft or misuse of personal data. The bill makes using electronic communications for fraud a separate crime and criminalizes establishing, operating, working for, or recruiting people for scam call centers. Convicted organizers or workers could face seven to 12 years in prison, pending President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s signature.

The legislation advanced after an anti-corruption investigation alleged that officials in the Prosecutor General’s Office took bribes from scam centers in exchange for protection from law enforcement. Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau named five suspects, while former Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko denied the allegations and has not been charged. Ukrainian authorities have also conducted operational crackdowns, including the shutdown of 94 suspected call centers after 411 searches and a Kyiv case involving more than $500,000 allegedly stolen from dozens of Americans through fictitious investment schemes.

  • The proposed law targets the full staffing pipeline of scam call centers, explicitly covering organizers, employees, and recruiters rather than only the people who directly contact victims.
  • The anti-corruption investigation alleges that the protection of scam operations involved officials inside the Prosecutor General’s Office, making enforcement corruption part of the issue addressed by the legislative push.
  • Ukraine-based call centers have targeted victims beyond Ukraine, including dozens of Americans in one Kyiv case, and have recruited English-speaking workers from the United States, West Africa, and European countries.
  • The reported shutdown of 94 suspected call centers during 411 searches shows that Ukrainian authorities describe the problem as widespread enough to require coordinated nationwide operations.

In plain words

A fake IRS email was sent to a commercial construction contractor and made to look official with government-style formatting and a download button. It gave itself away by claiming to be about a tax document that could not yet exist, because the tax return it referred to had not been filed. This matters because convincing-looking scam emails can pressure employees to click harmful links, but simply checking whether the message’s dates and claims make sense can reveal the fraud.

Summary
A phishing email impersonating the IRS exposed itself through an impossible CP2000 tax-year claim: it referenced a return that could not yet have been filed or reconciled. The case shows that checking internal inconsistencies in authoritative-looking messages can identify fraud before analyzing links or headers.

A phishing email impersonating the IRS reached a commercial construction contractor with a government-style header, logo, detail table, public IRS phone number, and a “Download Your Document” button. It contradicted itself by referring to a document for the “2026 filing year” while its table named a “CP2000 Notice - Tax Year 2026.” The article explains that a CP2000 compares a filed return against third-party reporting, so it cannot be issued for a tax year whose return has not yet been filed.

The sender used the display name “IRS.GOV” on an unrelated, long-established domain, while the visible To field was a fabricated no-reply address and the real recipient was delivered BCC-style. SPF passed for the sending domain, but no DKIM signature or DMARC result appeared, and the article stresses that authentication of the unrelated sender did not validate the IRS identity in the message. The sole button led to attacker-registered imahdyirs.es behind a shared CDN proxy, which returned a 403 response to scanning; IRONSCALES quarantined the message roughly seven seconds after receipt based on its malicious-link verdict, language and structure analysis, and community resolutions of similar incidents.

  • The forged notice was most easily disproved by the precise details intended to make it credible: its formal table contained claims that could be checked against each other and against the tax calendar.
  • A clean SPF result for a long-established sending domain did not validate the IRS identity, because the authentication applied to the unrelated sending domain rather than the agency named in the message.
  • The attacker avoided hosted images by embedding the IRS-style logo directly in the email as base64 data, leaving no remote image or tracking pixel to inspect.
  • The destination site’s 403 response meant the scanner did not observe its final content, so the article cautions against assuming what the link would have served.
  • The visible recipient field was fabricated to repeat the IRS brand while the actual target was delivered BCC-style, showing that email address fields a reader sees may not identify the real recipient.
Key Points
  • 01The phishing email impersonated the IRS and contained conflicting claims about a “2026 filing year” and a “CP2000 Notice - Tax Year 2026.”
  • 02A CP2000 notice compares a filed tax return with third-party reporting, so the article states that it cannot exist before the return for the named tax year has been filed.
  • 03The message used the display name “IRS.GOV” on an unrelated sending domain and placed the real recipient only in the envelope and delivery header.
  • 04The email’s single download button linked to imahdyirs.es, which was behind a shared CDN proxy and returned a 403 response to the scanner.
  • 05IRONSCALES quarantined the message roughly seven seconds after receipt based on its malicious-link verdict, language and structure analysis, and community resolutions of similar incidents.

AI-assisted code analysis is increasing the discovery of software flaws, placing unsupported or otherwise unpatchable systems at greater risk. This is especially significant for operational technology such as medical equipment, building management systems, and industrial systems in chemical plants, which may be certified for a fixed software configuration or run unsupported platforms. When patches cannot be applied, the article recommends using the predictable network behavior of OT systems as a compensating defense. Organizations should first identify legacy systems, then isolate them with VLANs and access control lists so that only authorized devices can communicate with them. Next-generation firewalls with current intrusion prevention capabilities can inspect traffic and block known exploit attempts before they reach vulnerable devices, while air gaps and one-way data-transfer devices should not be assumed to provide permanent separation because operational shortcuts can undermine them.

  • The same predictable communication patterns that make OT systems inflexible can be used defensively, because many of these systems only need to communicate with a small, known set of devices.

  • Air gaps and one-way data-transfer hardware may fail in practice when operational convenience leads staff or contractors to add temporary network connections that become lasting shortcuts.

BleepingComputer will host a live webinar with Material Security on September 23, 2026, titled “Breach autopsy: How fast-growing companies are breached through Google Workspace.” Material Security Vice President of Security Rajan Kapoor and Fireside Consulting LLC President Rick Fitzgerald will discuss real, publicly documented Google Workspace breaches. The session will focus on the decisions organizations made during the critical first hours after discovering suspicious access.

The webinar will examine two attacks in which threat actors combined social engineering with malicious OAuth applications to access Google Workspace environments. It will address how teams determine what users, data, and connected applications may have been exposed, whether an attacker retains access, and how to contain the incident. The speakers will also discuss response decisions that can limit or worsen an incident’s effects and the security controls they believe provide the greatest value for fast-growing companies with limited security resources.

  • Malicious OAuth applications can be combined with social engineering to obtain access, meaning connected applications are a potential source of exposure alongside user accounts and data.
  • Fast-growing companies with lean security teams face a particular challenge because they must investigate and contain an incident at the same time.

pwn-request technique

QR code concept

Quantum threat-actor
A ransomware threat-actor group referenced in security reporting.
quantum computers concept

quarantined concept

ransomware concept

read concept

real-world attacks concept

recommendation concept

reconnaissance technique

Recorded Future is one of the organizations named in the article.

The act of finding and persuading people to join an organization or activity.
redirect concept

regulators organization

relay concept

remote access concept

repositories concept

researchers organization

resilience concept

AI systems or automated agents that act outside intended rules, permissions, or user expectations.

run code concept

sabotage technique

sanctions concept

scams concept
